statement: Let $R \subseteq X \times Y$ be a [relation](c:relation) between finite sets. Let $K$ be the [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) on $X$ whose simplices are the nonempty sets of $X$ with a common partner $y \in Y$, and let $L$ be the same complex on $Y$ for the transposed relation. Then $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: The set $R \subseteq X \times Y$ is a [relation](c:relation) between the sets $X$ and $Y$.

conclusion: The geometric realizations $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

proofs.name: Nerve theorem
proofs.slogan: Cover $K$ by the full simplices on the sets $R(y)$, identify the nerve of this cover with $L$, and apply the nerve theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $X$ and $Y$. A point without any related partner lies in neither complex and is ignored.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines the sets $A_y$ that cover $K$, and the same sets define the nerve $L$.
Finiteness makes every full simplex finite and the cover finite, so the nerve theorem applies to finite complexes.

steps.slogan: Cover $K$ by the full simplices on the sets $A_y$.
steps.detail: For $y \in Y$ let $A_y = \{x : x \mathrel{R} y\}$ and let $\Delta_y$ be the full [simplex](c:simplex) on $A_y$. Every subset of $A_y$ has the common partner $y$, so $\Delta_y \subseteq K$. Every simplex of $K$ has a common partner $y$, so it lies in $\Delta_y$. Hence $K = \bigcup_y \Delta_y$.

steps.slogan: Compute each finite intersection of the cover sets as a full simplex.
steps.detail: The intersection $\Delta_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap \Delta_{y_k}$ is the full simplex on $A_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap A_{y_k}$. This set is nonempty exactly when some $x$ is related to every $y_i$. A full simplex is [contractible](c:contractible-space), so every nonempty finite intersection is contractible.

steps.slogan: Identify the nerve of the cover with the complex $L$.
steps.detail: The nerve has one vertex $y$ for each nonempty $\Delta_y$, and $\{y_0, \dots, y_k\}$ is a simplex exactly when $\Delta_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap \Delta_{y_k} \neq \emptyset$. By step 2 this means that some $x$ is related to every $y_i$, which is the definition of $L$.

steps.slogan: Apply the nerve theorem to $K$ and its cover to get $|K| \simeq |L|$.
steps.detail: A [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) covered by subcomplexes with contractible nonempty finite intersections is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the cover. Steps 1 and 2 give the hypotheses, and step 3 shows that the nerve is $L$. So $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

concepts.c:relation: The relation supplies the sets $A_y$ for the cover and the transposed complex.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: Both $K$ and $L$ are simplicial complexes, and $K$ is covered by subcomplexes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The nerve theorem gives the homotopy equivalence between $|K|$ and the nerve.
concepts.c:simplex: Each cover set is a full simplex, which has a simple intersection pattern.
concepts.c:contractible-space: Contractible intersections are the hypothesis of the nerve theorem.

source.note: The nerve theorem proof of Dowker duality, as in Bjorner, Topological methods, Handbook of Combinatorics (1995), section 10.

proofs.name: Galois connection of face posets
proofs.slogan: Pass to the posets of simplices, match them by the two Galois-connected maps $N$ and $M$, and use that comparable maps are homotopic.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $X$ and $Y$. The proof uses no nerve theorem and gives an explicit homotopy equivalence of the subdivisions.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines the maps $N$ and $M$ and the equivalence $\sigma \subseteq M(\tau) \iff \tau \subseteq N(\sigma)$.
Finiteness makes the sets $N(\sigma)$ and $M(\tau)$ finite, so they are simplices.

steps.slogan: Replace each complex by the poset of its simplices.
steps.detail: Let $F(K)$ be the poset of nonempty simplices of $K$ under inclusion, and define $F(L)$ in the same way. The order complex of $F(K)$ is the barycentric subdivision of $K$, so $|F(K)| \cong |K|$. Likewise $|F(L)| \cong |L|$, and the order complex of a poset equals that of its opposite.

steps.slogan: Define $N(\sigma)$ and $M(\tau)$ as the common partners of a simplex.
steps.detail: For $\sigma \in F(K)$ let $N(\sigma) = \{y : x \mathrel{R} y \text{ for all } x \in \sigma\}$. It is nonempty and finite, and any $x \in \sigma$ is a common partner of its subsets, so $N(\sigma) \in F(L)$. Define $M(\tau)$ symmetrically. Both maps reverse inclusion.

steps.slogan: Check that $\sigma \subseteq M(\tau)$ holds exactly when $\tau \subseteq N(\sigma)$.
steps.detail: Both conditions say that $x \mathrel{R} y$ for all $x \in \sigma$ and $y \in \tau$. Hence $\sigma \subseteq M(N(\sigma))$ and $\tau \subseteq N(M(\tau))$. The composite $M \circ N$ reverses inclusion twice, so it preserves it, and the same holds for $N \circ M$.

steps.slogan: Show that comparable order-preserving maps give homotopic maps of order complexes.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi \le \psi$ be order-preserving maps $P \to Q$. The map $P \times \{0 < 1\} \to Q$ that sends $(p,0)$ to $\varphi(p)$ and $(p,1)$ to $\psi(p)$ is order-preserving, and it gives a homotopy from $|\varphi|$ to $|\psi|$ on order complexes. So $|M \circ N| \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $|N \circ M| \simeq \mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $N$ and $M$ are inverse homotopy equivalences between the two order complexes.
steps.detail: The map $N$ is order-preserving from $F(K)$ to the opposite poset of $F(L)$, and $M$ goes back. By step 4 their composites are homotopic to the identity. So $|K| \cong |F(K)| \simeq |F(L)| \cong |L|$, which is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

concepts.c:relation: The relation defines both Galois-connected maps between the two posets.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The posets are the face posets of the two simplicial complexes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The maps $N$ and $M$ give the homotopy equivalence of the theorem.

source.note: The Galois connection proof (Quillen's comparable-maps lemma applied to face posets), as in Bjorner, Topological methods, Handbook of Combinatorics (1995), section 10.

statement: Let $R \subseteq X \times Y$ be a [relation](c:relation) between sets. The [Vietoris complex](c:vietoris-complex) $V$ on $X$ has as simplices the finite nonempty sets with a common $R$-partner in $Y$. The [Čech nerve](c:cech-nerve) $C$ of the sets $\{x : x \mathrel{R} y\}$ is the same complex on $Y$. Then $V$ and $C$ have isomorphic [homology](c:homology) in every degree.

hypotheses.text: The set $R \subseteq X \times Y$ is a [relation](c:relation) between two arbitrary sets $X$ and $Y$.

proofs.name: Double complex of the relation
proofs.slogan: Build the double complex of pairs of tuples that are all related, and show that both projections are quasi-isomorphisms.
proofs.scope: Homology with integer coefficients, for sets of any size. The homotopy equivalence for finite sets is the member treated at the record Dowker duality.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines both complexes and the double complex $B_{p,q}$, and its symmetry exchanges the two projections.

steps.slogan: Form the double complex $B_{p,q}$ of pairs of related tuples.
steps.detail: Let $C_p(V)$ be the free abelian group on tuples $(x_0, \dots, x_p)$ with a common partner, with the alternating face boundary. It computes $H_*(V)$. Define $C_*(C)$ likewise on $Y$. Let $B_{p,q}$ be the free abelian group on pairs of tuples $(x_0..x_p; y_0..y_q)$ with $x_i \mathrel{R} y_j$ for all $i, j$, with boundaries $d'$ on the $x$-part and $d''$ on the $y$-part.

steps.slogan: Show that each column over a fixed $x$-tuple is acyclic.
steps.detail: Fix $a = (x_0, \dots, x_p)$ in $C_p(V)$ and let $N(a)$ be its nonempty set of common partners. The column over $a$ is the complex $\mathbb{Z}[N(a)^{q+1}]$. Pick $y^* \in N(a)$. Then $h(y_0, \dots, y_q) = (y^*, y_0, \dots, y_q)$ is a contracting homotopy of the augmented column, so its homology is $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $0$ only.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the projection $\mathrm{Tot}\,B \to C_*(V)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The projection sends a pair $(a; y_0)$ to $a$ and the pairs with $q > 0$ to $0$. The columns have homology $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $0$, so the standard spectral sequence of a first-quadrant [double complex](c:chain-complex) collapses. Hence the projection is an isomorphism on [homology](c:homology).

steps.slogan: Repeat the argument for rows to get $\mathrm{Tot}\,B \to C_*(C)$ as a quasi-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The definition of $B_{p,q}$ is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, because $R$ and its transpose define it in the same way. Steps 2 and 3 with the roles exchanged show that each row is acyclic and that the projection to $C_*(C)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Compose the two quasi-isomorphisms to identify $H_n(V)$ with $H_n(C)$.
steps.detail: Both projections induce isomorphisms from $H_n(\mathrm{Tot}\,B)$. Therefore $H_n(V) \cong H_n(\mathrm{Tot}\,B) \cong H_n(C)$ for every $n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:relation: The relation defines both complexes and the symmetric double complex.
concepts.c:vietoris-complex: The Vietoris complex $V$ is one side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:cech-nerve: The Čech nerve $C$ is the other side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:homology: The proof compares the homology groups of the two complexes through a third complex.
concepts.c:chain-complex: The double complex is a family of chain complexes with a total complex.

source.note: The standard double complex argument for C. H. Dowker, Homology groups of relations, Annals of Mathematics 56 (1952), 84-95, which proves the theorem.

statement: Every finite simple [planar graph](c:planar-graph) has a proper vertex [colouring](c:graph-coloring) with at most five colours, so adjacent vertices get different colours.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph), that is, it has a drawing in the plane without crossing edges.
The graph $G$ is finite and simple: it has no loops and no multiple edges.

conclusion: The vertices of $G$ can be coloured with colours $1, \dots, 5$ so that adjacent vertices have different colours.

proofs.name: Kempe chains
proofs.slogan: Remove a vertex of degree at most five, colour the rest by induction, and free a colour for it by swapping along a Kempe chain.
proofs.scope: Induction on the number of vertices, with at most five vertices as the base case. The map form follows by taking the dual graph, whose vertices are the regions of the map.

roles.why: Planarity gives Euler's formula and a vertex of small degree, keeps $G - v$ planar, and lets the Jordan curve theorem separate two neighbours.
Simplicity gives the edge bound $3n - 6$, and finiteness makes the induction on the vertex count work.

steps.slogan: Find a vertex of degree at most five by Euler's formula.
steps.detail: A simple [planar graph](c:planar-graph) with $n \ge 3$ vertices has at most $3n - 6$ edges, because every face has at least three edges and $V - E + F = 2$. The degree sum $2E \le 6n - 12$ is below $6n$, so some vertex $v$ has degree at most $5$.

steps.slogan: Delete the vertex $v$ and colour the smaller graph by induction.
steps.detail: The graph $G - v$ is simple and planar with fewer vertices. By the induction hypothesis it has a proper [colouring](c:graph-coloring) with colours $1, \dots, 5$. It remains to extend this colouring to $v$, after a recolouring if needed.

steps.slogan: Colour $v$ directly when its neighbours leave a colour unused.
steps.detail: If $v$ has at most four neighbours, or its neighbours use at most four colours, a free colour exists and the colouring extends. Otherwise $v$ has exactly five neighbours $v_1, \dots, v_5$, in this cyclic order around $v$ in the drawing, and they carry the colours $1, \dots, 5$.

steps.slogan: Swap colours 1 and 3 along the Kempe chain of $v_1$ if it misses $v_3$.
steps.detail: Let $K$ be the component of $v_1$ in the subgraph induced by the vertices of colour 1 or 3. This is a [Kempe chain](c:kempe-chain). If $v_3 \notin K$, exchange the two colours on $K$. The colouring stays proper, $v_1$ gets colour 3, no neighbour of $v$ has colour 1, and $v$ takes colour 1.

steps.slogan: Otherwise separate $v_2$ from $v_4$ by a closed curve and swap colours 2 and 4.
steps.detail: If $v_3 \in K$, a path of colours 1 and 3 from $v_1$ to $v_3$ together with $v$ forms a cycle. By the Jordan curve theorem it separates $v_2$ from $v_4$, so the 2-4 [Kempe chain](c:kempe-chain) of $v_2$ misses $v_4$. Swapping colours 2 and 4 on it frees colour 2 for $v$. Every case gives a proper 5-colouring.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Planarity gives a vertex of degree at most five and the separating cycle.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: The proof extends a proper colouring from $G - v$ to $G$.
concepts.c:kempe-chain: Swapping two colours along a Kempe chain keeps the colouring proper and frees a colour.

source.note: Heawood's 1890 proof (P. J. Heawood, Map-colour theorem, Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 24, 332-338), which repairs Kempe's argument; found in standard graph theory texts.

statement: Let $P$ be a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup) of a finite group $G$. Let the focal subgroup $P^*$ be generated by the commutators $[x, g] = x^{-1} g^{-1} x g$ with $x \in P$ and $g \in G$ that lie in $P$. Then $P \cap [G, G] = P^*$.

hypotheses.text: The subgroup $P$ is a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $p$-subgroup of $G$ for a prime $p$.

conclusion: The intersection of $P$ with the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) $[G, G]$ equals the focal subgroup $P^*$.

formal.difference: The declaration assumes only that $P$ has finite index in $G$, so $G$ may be infinite. It states the same equality.

proofs.name: Transfer to $P/P^*$
proofs.slogan: Transfer $G$ into the abelian $p$-group $P/P^*$, where the transfer acts on $P$ as a power map prime to $p$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The inclusion $P^* \le P \cap [G,G]$ is direct, and the reverse inclusion uses the transfer.

roles.why: A [finite group](c:finite-group) has a Sylow subgroup of finite index, so the transfer exists and its power formula uses the index $[G:P]$.
The Sylow subgroup makes $P/P^*$ a $p$-group and makes the index $[G:P]$ prime to $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the focal subgroup lies in $P$ and in the commutator subgroup.
steps.detail: Each generator $[x, g]$ is a commutator of $G$, so $P^* \le [G, G]$. Each generator lies in $P$ by definition, so $P^* \le P$. Hence $P^* \le P \cap [G, G]$.

steps.slogan: Form the abelian quotient $P/P^*$ that receives the transfer.
steps.detail: For $a, b \in P$ the commutator $[a, b]$ lies in $P$, so it is a generator of $P^*$. Hence $[P, P] \le P^*$ and $P/P^*$ is abelian. It is also a $p$-group, as a quotient of $P$.

steps.slogan: Define the [transfer homomorphism](c:transfer-homomorphism) $V \colon G \to P/P^*$ and kill $[G, G]$ with it.
steps.detail: Because $[G:P]$ is finite, the transfer into the abelian group $P/P^*$ is a homomorphism $V$. Its target is abelian, so $V$ is trivial on $[G, G]$. Hence $[G, G] \le \ker V$.

steps.slogan: Compute $V(x)$ for $x \in P$ as the power $x^{[G:P]}$ modulo $P^*$.
steps.detail: Let $\langle x \rangle$ act on the cosets $G/P$ by left multiplication. The transfer $V(x)$ is the product over the orbits of terms $g^{-1} x^m g$, where $m$ is the orbit size. Each term lies in $P$ and is congruent to $x^m$ modulo $P^*$. The orbit sizes sum to $[G:P]$, so $V(x) \equiv x^{[G:P]}$.

steps.slogan: Show $P \cap \ker V = P^*$ because the index $[G:P]$ is prime to $p$.
steps.detail: If $x \in P$ and $V(x) = 1$, then $x^{[G:P]} \in P^*$. In the $p$-group $P/P^*$ the power map by an integer prime to $p$ is injective, so $x \in P^*$. Thus $P \cap [G, G] \le P \cap \ker V \le P^* \le P \cap [G, G]$ by step 1.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives a finite index and a well-defined transfer.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The index of a Sylow subgroup is prime to $p$.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The transfer kills the commutator subgroup, and the theorem identifies its part in $P$.
concepts.c:transfer-homomorphism: The transfer maps $G$ to $P/P^*$ and restricts to a power map on $P$.
